title: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
summary: Why decoding is memory bound, how a cheap draft plus one target pass keeps the target's exact distribution, the speedup math, a working implementation, Medusa, EAGLE, self-speculation, and serving at scale.
outcomes: Explain why verifying several guessed tokens costs about one decode step at small batch size
Prove with numbers that min(1, p/q) acceptance plus residual resampling yields exactly the target distribution
Compute expected tokens per round and walltime speedup from alpha, gamma, the cost ratio c and the measured verify cost
Implement speculative sampling with KV-cache rollback and test it for exactness and speed
Explain how Medusa heads, token trees and EAGLE's feature-level drafter raise acceptance
Compare self-speculative drafts: MTP modules, layer skipping and lookahead decoding
Predict when speculation helps or hurts a batched server from batch size, context length and gamma

lessons.title: Why decoding is slow and why checking guesses is cheap

blocks.md: Recall from GPU and inference basics: generating text runs the model once per new token, and at small batch sizes each of those decode steps is limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic. Every step streams all the weights (and the KV cache) from GPU memory to produce a single token per sequence.

Chen et al. (DeepMind) put a number on this ceiling: since all parameters must pass through the chips once per step, *model size divided by total memory bandwidth* is a hard lower bound on time per token for plain autoregressive sampling (one token per forward pass, each new token fed back in as input for the next). In their setup Chinchilla 70B (DeepMind's 70-billion-parameter language model) on 16 TPU v4 chips (Google's machine learning accelerators) took **14.1 ms per token**.

The key observation behind speculative decoding is about *scoring*, not generating. Call the big model whose outputs we want the **target**, and a much smaller, cheaper model that proposes guesses the **draft** model. Given a prefix plus a short guessed continuation of $K$ tokens, one forward pass of the big model returns the next-token distribution at every one of those positions, exactly as it does during training or prefill. Chen et al. argue this costs about the same as producing one token when $K$ is small, because each part of the step stays memory bound:

- **Linear layers**: the weights are read once whether they multiply 1 or 5 token vectors.
- **Attention**: the dominant cost is reading the KV cache, which does not grow with $K$. The $K$ extra query rows do add arithmetic, about $4\,n_{\text{layer}}\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,d$ FLOPs each (the count from GPU and inference basics): 2.15 GFLOP per row for LLaMA-7B at 4,096 tokens of context, against 2.15 GB of cache read once. That is about $K$ FLOPs per byte, far below an A100's ridge of about 153, so for one sequence it is noise. It starts to cost real time once batch x $(K+1)$ rows in the linear layers approach that ridge (lesson 9).
- **All-reduces** between chips: each of the 16 chips holds a slice of every weight matrix, so the chips must exchange and sum their partial results, an operation called an all-reduce that leaves every chip with the total. For a handful of token vectors the messages are tiny, so the time is set by the fixed delay of each exchange (latency bound), not by message size, either way.

blocks.title: Five tokens: plain decoding vs one speculative round

scenes.caption: Plain decoding: five sequential target steps at 14.1 ms each (Chinchilla 70B timing from Chen et al.) give five tokens in 70.5 ms.
Speculative round: a small draft model (1.8 ms per token in Chen et al.) guesses 4 tokens in 7.2 ms. Nothing is output yet; these are only guesses.

One target pass scores all 4 guesses plus one extra position, assumed to cost one ordinary step (14.1 ms). The round ends at 21.3 ms and yields between 1 and 5 tokens. Simplified: real verification is slightly slower than one step.

If all 5 tokens are kept, that is 4.26 ms per token against 14.1 ms. If the first guess is wrong, the round still gives 1 token, at 21.3 ms instead of 14.1 ms. The payoff depends on how often guesses survive.

blocks.md: This is speculative execution, the CPU trick of doing work before you know it is needed, applied to language models. Two groups published it independently: Leviathan, Kalman and Matias at Google (**speculative decoding**, 2022) and Chen et al. at DeepMind (**speculative sampling**, 2023).

Why not simply use a smaller model? Because it changes the answers. Distillation (training a small student model to imitate the big model's outputs) and quantization (storing the weights in fewer bits, say 8 instead of 16) trade quality for speed: each gives you a different model whose answers can differ. Speculative decoding makes a stronger promise: the tokens you get are distributed **exactly** as if the target had generated them alone. The draft only decides how many target steps you can skip.

Decoding is slow because each step moves all the weights to produce one token. Checking $K$ guessed tokens in one target pass moves the weights once, so every accepted guess is a target step you did not pay for.

blocks.prompt: A draft guesses 4 tokens and the target rejects the very first one. How many tokens does that round output: 0, or at least 1?
blocks.reveal: At least 1. The verify pass already computed the target's own distribution at the first position, so on a rejection the algorithm samples a replacement token from it (lesson 3 shows exactly which distribution). A round therefore never produces fewer tokens than a plain decode step; the risk is only the wasted draft time.

blocks.question: Why can the target model score 5 guessed tokens in roughly the time it takes to generate 1 token at batch size 1?
options: The target skips attention for guessed tokens
Guessed tokens use a lower precision path
The GPU runs 5 separate copies of the model in parallel
At small batch the step is memory bound: weights and KV cache are read once either way, and 5 token vectors add little arithmetic
blocks.explain: The cost of a small-batch decode step is dominated by reading weights and KV cache from memory. Multiplying those weights by 5 vectors instead of 1 adds arithmetic the chip has to spare, so latency barely changes (Chen et al.'s argument for linear layers, attention and all-reduces).

blocks.question: Which claim about speculative decoding is correct?
options: It speeds up decoding by letting a smaller model answer the easy prompts
It trades a small amount of quality for latency, like quantization
It produces the same output distribution as the target model and only changes how many target passes are needed
It only works with greedy decoding
blocks.explain: Both original papers prove the sampled tokens follow the target's distribution for any draft. Quality is unchanged; speed depends on how well the draft guesses. Lesson 3 covers sampling, not just greedy.

lessons.title: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding

blocks.md: Start with greedy decoding (temperature 0), where the target always picks its most likely token. Temperature $T$ divides the model's raw scores (logits) before the softmax: $T$ above 1 flattens the distribution, $T$ below 1 sharpens it, and as $T$ goes to 0 all probability lands on the top score, so sampling becomes taking the argmax, the token with the largest probability. Then verification is just a comparison: a guessed token is correct if and only if it equals the target's argmax at that position. One round of the loop with lookahead $\gamma$ (Leviathan's name; Chen calls it $K$) goes like this:

1. **Draft**: run the draft model $\gamma$ times autoregressively to get guesses $x_1, \dots, x_\gamma$.
2. **Score**: run the target once on prefix plus all $\gamma$ guesses. Because attention is causal, position $i$ sees only the prefix and $x_1..x_{i-1}$, so the pass returns $\gamma + 1$ next-token distributions $p_1, \dots, p_{\gamma+1}$.
3. **Verify** left to right: keep guesses while they match the target; stop at the first mismatch.
4. **Fix up**: append the target's own token at the first mismatch, or if every guess matched, a **bonus** token from $p_{\gamma+1}$.

blocks.title: Two rounds of speculative decoding with gamma = 4

scenes.caption: The engine asks the draft for 4 guesses after the prefix 'the cat'. The draft runs 4 cheap sequential steps.
One target forward pass over prefix plus 4 guesses returns 5 distributions: one for each guess position and one extra after 'mat'.
Compare: 'sat' and 'on' match, 'a' does not. Keep 2 guesses, replace 'a' with the target's 'the', and drop 'mat'. Three tokens from one target pass.

Next round starts from the longer prefix. Both caches drop their entries for rejected positions: the target's verify pass also wrote keys and values for 'a' and 'mat', and they must be cut off (lesson 5 shows the call).
All 4 guesses match, so the algorithm also takes the bonus token 'warm' from the fifth distribution: 5 tokens from one target pass, the maximum of gamma + 1.

blocks.title: Round 1 position by position

scenes.caption: The target pass gives its argmax at all 5 positions at once. Position 4 (the bonus slot) has no guess; it is only used if every guess survives.
Positions 0 and 1 match, so both guesses are accepted. They cost one draft step each and no extra target step.
Position 2 mismatches: 'a' is rejected and the target's 'the' is written instead. Everything after it, 'mat' and the target's 'floor', is thrown away because it was computed for the wrong prefix.

blocks.md: Two properties fall out of the structure. First, every round outputs **at least one** target token, so the number of sequential target passes can never exceed plain decoding. Second, a round outputs **at most** $\gamma + 1$ tokens. The cost you risk on a bad round is the $\gamma$ draft steps plus any slowdown of the wider verify pass.

The idea of checking several predicted tokens with one pass is older than both 2022 papers: Stern, Shazeer and Uszkoreit's blockwise parallel decoding (2018) did it for greedy decoding: predict several steps in parallel, then keep the longest prefix the scoring model validates. What Leviathan et al. and Chen et al. added is a verification rule that works for **sampling** at any temperature, which is the next lesson.

A common bug: after a rejection, keeping the target's distributions for later positions. Those were computed with the rejected guess in the context, so they condition on a token that is no longer in the output. Only the distribution at the first rejected position is valid. Cache state has the same trap: the verify pass appended keys and values for every guess to the target's KV cache, so after a rejection the cache must be cut back to the accepted length before the next round.

blocks.question: A round with gamma = 5 finds the first mismatch at guess 4 (1-based). How many tokens does it append?
blocks.explain: Guesses 1 to 3 are accepted and the target's own token replaces guess 4, giving 4 tokens. Guess 5 and the bonus slot are discarded because they were computed after a rejected token.

blocks.question: Why does the target pass produce gamma + 1 distributions rather than gamma?
options: Causal attention gives a next-token distribution after every input token, including after the last guess, which supplies a bonus token when all guesses pass
One extra position is needed to check the prefix
The draft also returns one distribution that is reused
It is an implementation detail that is never used
blocks.explain: The forward pass over prefix plus gamma guesses outputs a distribution after each of them. The last one, after guess gamma, is a free target prediction used only when all guesses are accepted, raising the maximum to gamma + 1 tokens per round.

lessons.title: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution

blocks.md: With sampling, 'does the guess match' no longer makes sense: the target might have produced several tokens. We need a rule that accepts a guess $x$ drawn from the draft distribution $q$ in such a way that the final token is drawn from the target distribution $p$. Notation follows Leviathan et al.: $p$ is the target, $q$ the draft. (Chen et al. use the opposite letters, so read carefully when comparing.)

The rule is a modified **rejection sampler**. Classic rejection sampling draws from an easy distribution and keeps each draw with a carefully chosen probability, so that the kept draws follow a harder one; here the easy one is the draft and the hard one is the target. Sample $x \sim q$. Accept it with probability $\min(1, p(x)/q(x))$: always if the target likes $x$ at least as much as the draft does, otherwise in proportion. In code you draw a uniform random number $u$ between 0 and 1 and accept when $u$ is below that ratio. If rejected, sample a replacement from the **residual** distribution, the part of $p$ that the draft under-covers:

blocks.tex: P(\text{accept } x) = \min\!\left(1, \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right), \qquad p'(x) = \frac{\max(0,\, p(x) - q(x))}{\sum_{y} \max(0,\, p(y) - q(y))}
blocks.caption: In words: accept x with probability p(x) over q(x), capped at 1. On rejection, take p minus q wherever it is positive, set the rest to 0, and divide by the total so it sums to 1.

blocks.md: Temperature, top-k and nucleus sampling are applied to both $p$ and $q$ first; the rule works on whatever adjusted distributions you sample from. **Top-k** keeps only the k most likely tokens and rescales them to sum to 1. **Nucleus** sampling (also called top-p, a different p from the target's) keeps the smallest set of most likely tokens whose probabilities add up to at least a threshold such as 0.9, then rescales.

A concrete case on a 4-token vocabulary {the, a, cat, dog}. Target $p = (0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1)$, draft $q = (0.3, 0.4, 0.1, 0.2)$. The draft over-proposes 'a' and 'dog', so those are the only tokens that can be rejected, each with acceptance probability $0.5$. The draft under-proposes 'the' and 'cat', so the residual puts all its mass there.

blocks.title: Toy vocabulary: how acceptance plus residual rebuilds p

scenes.caption: Target distribution p, the one we must sample from: 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1.
Draft distribution q: 0.3, 0.4, 0.1, 0.2. Cheap to sample but wrong. Acceptance probabilities min(1, p/q) are 1, 0.5, 1, 0.5.
Probability of proposing x AND accepting it: q(x) min(1, p/q) = min(p, q) = 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1. Total acceptance probability is 0.7.
Rejection happens with probability 0.3. The residual max(0, p - q) = (0.2, 0, 0.1, 0) also sums to 0.3, normalized to (2/3, 0, 1/3, 0). Mass contributed: 0.2, 0, 0.1, 0.
Accepted mass plus residual mass: 0.3 + 0.2, 0.2 + 0, 0.1 + 0.1, 0.1 + 0 = 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1. Exactly p. A 200,000-sample simulation gives 0.501, 0.201, 0.199, 0.099.

Contrast a plausible wrong rule: accept only if q(x) is at most p(x), else resample from p. It outputs 0.6, 0.12, 0.22, 0.06, biased toward 'the'. Resampling from p instead of the residual double counts.

blocks.md: The general proof is the same two terms. The chance of outputting $x$ is the chance of proposing and accepting it, plus the chance of rejecting anything times the residual's probability of $x$. For every token, $\max(0, p - q) = p - \min(p, q)$ (if $p$ is larger both sides are $p - q$, otherwise both are 0), and $p$ sums to 1, so $\sum_y \max(0, p - q) = 1 - \sum_y \min(p, q)$. That is exactly the rejection probability, so the residual's normalizer cancels it:

blocks.tex: P(X = x) = \underbrace{\min(p(x), q(x))}_{\text{accepted}} + \Big(1 - \sum_y \min(p, q)\Big)\frac{p(x) - \min(p(x), q(x))}{1 - \sum_y \min(p, q)} = p(x)
blocks.caption: In words: the accepted mass min(p, q), plus the rejection probability times the residual. The rejection probability cancels the normalizer, leaving min(p, q) plus p minus min(p, q), which is p. Works for any q, however bad. A bad draft only lowers the acceptance probability, never the quality.

blocks.md: Leviathan et al. call this per-position acceptance probability $\beta = \sum_x \min(p(x), q(x))$ and its average over the text $\alpha = E[\beta]$, the **acceptance rate**. It is one minus the total variation distance between $p$ and $q$ (half the sum of the absolute differences $|p(x) - q(x)|$). The smaller of two numbers is half of their sum minus the gap between them, and each distribution sums to 1, so the summed minimums are 1 minus half the summed gaps: $\sum_x \min(p, q) = 1 - \frac{1}{2}\sum_x |p(x) - q(x)|$. So it is 1 when the models agree and 0 when their supports (the tokens each gives nonzero probability) are disjoint. For our toy pair, half of $0.2 + 0.2 + 0.1 + 0.1$ is 0.3, so $\beta = 0.7$.

blocks.prompt: Greedy decoding is the special case where p and q are one-hot (all probability on a single token). What does the acceptance rule reduce to?
blocks.reveal: With one-hot distributions, $p(x)/q(x)$ is 1 when the draft's token is the target's argmax and 0 otherwise, so the guess is accepted exactly when it matches. The residual $\max(0, p - q)$ is then one-hot on the target's argmax. That is the comparison rule from lesson 2, so greedy is not a separate algorithm.

blocks.title: Verifying the round 'sat on a mat' with sampling
blocks.code:
def verify(p, q, drafts, rand):
    # p[i], q[i]: target and draft distributions
    # at draft position i (dicts token to prob)
    out = []
    for i, x in enumerate(drafts):
        ratio = min(1.0, p[i][x] / q[i][x])
        if rand() < ratio:
            out.append(x)            # accept guess
            continue
        res = {t: max(0.0, p[i][t] - q[i].get(t, 0.0))
               for t in p[i]}
        z = sum(res.values())
        res = {t: v / z for t, v in res.items()}
        out.append(sample(res))      # fix-up token
        return out
    out.append(sample(p[len(drafts)]))  # bonus
    return out

scenes.caption: Guess 0 'sat': q = 0.6, p = 0.7. The target likes it more than the draft, so the ratio is clipped to 1 and it is always accepted.
Guess 1 'on': q = 0.8, p = 0.6, ratio 0.75. The uniform draw 0.42 is below 0.75, so it is accepted.
Guess 2 'a': q = 0.5, p = 0.2, ratio 0.4. The draw 0.81 exceeds 0.4: reject.
Residual at position 2. Over {the, a, my, his}: p = (0.6, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1), q = (0.3, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1), so max(0, p - q) = (0.3, 0, 0, 0). Normalized, 'the' has probability 1.
The fix-up token 'the' is appended and the round returns 3 tokens. 'mat' and the bonus distribution are never examined.

blocks.md: Speculative sampling is exact in math, not bit for bit. Chen et al. note samples match the target 'within hardware numerics': different batching, kernels and random number streams change floating point results, so a fixed seed will not reproduce plain decoding token for token.

Accept with $\min(1, p/q)$, on rejection sample from $\text{norm}(\max(0, p - q))$, where norm rescales to sum to 1. Accepted mass is $\min(p, q)$ and residual mass is $p - \min(p, q)$; they add up to $p$ for any draft.

blocks.question: Draft q = (0.7, 0.3) and target p = (0.4, 0.6) over two tokens {A, B}. The draft proposes A. What is the probability A is kept, and if not, what is sampled?
options: Kept with prob 0.4; otherwise sample from p
Kept with prob 4/7; otherwise output B with probability 1
Kept with prob 0.7; otherwise output B
Always kept, since A has nonzero target probability
blocks.explain: Acceptance is min(1, p(A)/q(A)) = 0.4/0.7 = 4/7. The residual max(0, p - q) = (0, 0.3) normalizes to B with probability 1. Check: P(A) = 0.7 x 4/7 = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3 + 0.7 x 3/7 = 0.6.

blocks.question: A teammate 'simplifies' the sampler: on rejection, sample the replacement from p instead of the residual. What happens?
options: Nothing; p and the residual are the same distribution
Outputs become biased toward tokens the draft under-proposes, because their accepted mass is counted twice
Outputs become biased toward tokens the draft over-proposes
Acceptance rate drops but outputs stay exact
blocks.explain: Rejection still happens with probability 0.3 in the toy example, but the replacement now follows p, so each token gets min(p, q) + 0.3 p(x): 0.45, 0.26, 0.16, 0.13 instead of 0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1. 'a' and 'dog', which the draft over-proposes, gain mass. The residual sends rejected mass only to under-covered tokens, adding exactly the missing p(x) - q(x).

blocks.question: Which pair of models has the higher acceptance rate beta for a single position?
options: Both are equal because both drafts put most mass on the first token
blocks.explain: beta = sum of min(p, q). First pair: 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6. Second pair: 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9. What matters is overlap with the target, not agreeing on the top token.

lessons.title: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect

blocks.md: Leviathan et al. model each guess as accepted independently with probability $\alpha$ (a simplification; real acceptance varies with context). A round then keeps guesses until the first rejection, capped at $\gamma$, and always adds one target token. The number of tokens per round is a **capped geometric** variable: geometric because it counts trials until the first failure, like flipping a biased coin until it lands tails, and capped because a round stops after $\gamma$ guesses.

blocks.title: Tokens produced by one round, alpha = 0.8, gamma = 4

scenes.caption: First guess rejected: probability 1 - 0.8 = 0.2, and the round still yields 1 target token.
k guesses accepted then a rejection has probability 0.8^k x 0.2: 0.16, 0.128, 0.1024 for k = 1, 2, 3.
All 4 accepted: 0.8^4 = 0.4096, giving 4 + 1 bonus = 5 tokens. The cap makes this the most likely outcome. Expected tokens: 3.36 per target pass.

blocks.md: Where 3.36 comes from: a round yields at least $k + 1$ tokens exactly when its first $k$ guesses are all accepted, which has probability $\alpha^k$, for $k$ from 0 to $\gamma$. The expected value of a count is the sum of the chances that it reaches 1, 2, 3 and so on, so the expected tokens are $S = 1 + \alpha + \alpha^2 + \dots + \alpha^\gamma$. For $\alpha = 0.8$ and $\gamma = 4$ that is $1 + 0.8 + 0.64 + 0.512 + 0.4096 = 3.36$. To close the sum, multiply $S$ by $\alpha$ and subtract it from $S$: every term cancels except the first and the last, leaving $1 - \alpha^{\gamma+1}$; divide that by $1 - \alpha$ and you get the formula below.

blocks.caption: In words: expected tokens equal one minus alpha to the power gamma plus 1, over one minus alpha (Leviathan et al., Equation 1). For alpha = 0.8 and gamma = 4 this is 3.36; as gamma grows, alpha to the power gamma plus 1 shrinks to 0, so it can never exceed 1 / (1 - alpha).

blocks.title: Expected tokens per target pass vs lookahead gamma

scenes.caption: alpha = 0.6: diminishing returns arrive fast. gamma = 2 gives 1.96 tokens, gamma = 10 only 2.49, close to the ceiling of 2.5.
alpha = 0.8: gamma = 2 gives 2.44, gamma = 5 gives 3.69 (matching Table 1 of the paper), and the ceiling is 5.
alpha = 0.9: the ceiling rises to 10 and long drafts keep paying: gamma = 10 gives 6.86 tokens per pass. Acceptance rate is the lever that matters most.

blocks.md: Tokens per pass is not yet speed, because drafting costs time. Leviathan et al. define the **cost coefficient** $c$ as the time of one draft step divided by one target step. A round costs $\gamma c + 1$ target-step units: $\gamma$ draft steps of $c$ each, plus one target pass (assuming the wide verify pass costs one step). Plain decoding makes 1 token per target step, so the expected walltime improvement is the expected tokens per round divided by this cost:

blocks.caption: Theorem 3.8. Assumes enough spare compute to verify gamma + 1 positions in one step, and long generations. Lesson 5 measures how far a real verify pass is from one step, and lesson 9 shows when batching breaks it.

blocks.title: Walltime speedup vs gamma for a draft costing c target steps

scenes.caption: alpha = 0.8, c = 0.05: the speedup peaks at gamma = 8 with 3.09x, then falls because each extra draft step costs more than the expected gain.
Same alpha with c = 0.128, the ratio of Chen et al.'s 1.8 ms draft to 14.1 ms target: the best gamma drops to 5 and the speedup to 2.25x.
alpha = 0.6, c = 0.05: best gamma 4, only 1.92x. A weaker draft wants shorter rounds.
alpha = 0.2, c = 0: like Leviathan's bigram drafter for translation (alpha about 0.2, free to run). gamma = 3 gives 1.25x, as the paper reports.

blocks.md: Two consequences from the paper. **Break-even**: if $\alpha > c$ some $\gamma$ gives a speedup, of at least $(1+\alpha)/(1+c)$ (Corollary 3.9): with $\gamma = 1$ a round yields $1 + \alpha$ tokens on average for $1 + c$ steps of time, a ratio above 1 exactly when $\alpha > c$. **Compute is not free**: each round the target processes $\gamma + 1$ positions and the draft $\gamma$ positions at $\hat c$ each, where $\hat c$ is the draft's arithmetic per token relative to the target. Dividing that work by the expected tokens per round, and comparing with 1 unit per token for plain decoding, total arithmetic grows by $(1-\alpha)(\gamma \hat{c} + \gamma + 1)/(1-\alpha^{\gamma+1})$. With a free draft, $\alpha = 0.8$ and $\gamma = 5$ give 3.69x speed for 1.63x the operations: 6 units of work per round over 3.69 tokens.

Measured numbers line up. On T5-XXL (11B) with a T5-small (77M) draft (T5 is Google's family of encoder-decoder transformers that cast every task as text in, text out), batch 1 on a TPU v4, Leviathan et al. measured $\alpha$ = 0.75 and a 3.4x speedup for English-German translation at temperature 0, and $\alpha$ = 0.62 and 2.6x at temperature 1. Chen et al. measured 1.92x to 2.46x on Chinchilla 70B with $K = 4$. Leviathan et al. saw higher acceptance at temperature 0 than at 1, and Chen et al. saw their largest gain on code (HumanEval, OpenAI's set of 164 Python programming problems checked by unit tests).

Speedup is not tokens per pass. A draft that is accurate but slow (high alpha, high c) can lose to a weaker but nearly free one. Leviathan et al. found drafts about two orders of magnitude smaller than the target usually balanced alpha and c best.

blocks.question: Your draft has alpha = 0.6 and c = 0.05. A colleague sets gamma = 10 'to get more tokens per pass'. Using the speedup formula, what happens?
options: Speedup rises to about 2.5x, the ceiling
Speedup is unchanged; gamma only affects throughput
Speedup falls to about 1.66x, below the 1.92x at gamma = 4
Decoding becomes slower than plain decoding
blocks.explain: Tokens per pass barely grow past gamma = 4 (2.31 to 2.49), but draft cost grows linearly: (1 - 0.6^11)/(0.4 x 1.5) = 1.66 versus 1.92 at gamma = 4. Still above 1, so not slower than plain decoding.

blocks.question: Which change raises the maximum achievable speedup when the draft is free (c = 0)?
options: Increasing gamma beyond 20
Lowering the target's temperature has no effect
Using a bigger GPU for the draft
Raising alpha, because the speedup is capped by 1/(1 - alpha)
blocks.explain: With c = 0 the speedup is the expected tokens per pass, bounded by 1/(1 - alpha) however large gamma gets. Only better acceptance raises the cap; lower temperature usually helps because it sharpens both distributions.

lessons.title: Build it: speculative sampling with two real models

blocks.md: Time to turn lessons 2 and 3 into code and test lesson 4's formula on real models. The pair comes from Hugging Face's SmolLM2 family: **SmolLM2-135M** drafts and **SmolLM2-360M** is the target. They share one tokenizer with 49,152 tokens, which the rule needs, because $p$ and $q$ must be distributions over the same vocabulary. Everything in this lesson ran on a laptop CPU (Apple M5 Pro, 2 threads, PyTorch 2.15, transformers 5.24), so you can rerun it without a GPU; GPU speedups in this course come from the papers.

Both models keep a **KV cache** (GPU and inference basics, lesson 5): the keys and values of every token already processed, so a forward pass only runs new tokens. The loop keeps one invariant: each cache holds every token of the accepted text except the last. `feed` runs exactly the tokens a cache has not seen yet, and `rollback` cuts a cache back to a given length. Rollback is the step the theory lessons skipped: the verify pass writes cache entries for every guess, rejected ones included, and so does the draft.

blocks.caption: Helpers. In transformers 4.x, crop(n) with a positive n kept n entries (a negative n already removed entries); current releases reject a positive n, so crop(-n) is the way to remove the last n.

blocks.title: One real round: SmolLM2 pair, gamma = 4, temperature 1
blocks.code:
def speculative(ids, n_new, gamma, T, g):
    seq, dc, tc = list(ids), DynamicCache(), DynamicCache()
    feed(target, tc, seq[:-1]); feed(draft, dc, seq[:-1])
    while len(seq) - len(ids) < n_new:
        guesses, qs = [], []
        for _ in range(gamma):                    # 1. draft
            q = probs(feed(draft, dc, seq + guesses)[-1], T)
            qs.append(q); guesses.append(sample(q, g))
        ps = probs(feed(target, tc, seq + guesses)[-(gamma + 1):], T)
        n = 0
        for i, x in enumerate(guesses):           # 3. accept or fix up
            u = torch.rand(1, generator=g).item()
            if u < min(1.0, (ps[i, x] / qs[i][x]).item()):
                n += 1
                continue
            res = torch.clamp(ps[i] - qs[i], min=0)
            extra = sample(res / res.sum(), g)
            break
        else:
            extra = sample(ps[gamma], g)          # bonus token
        seq += guesses[:n] + [extra]
        rollback(tc, len(seq) - 1)                # 4. roll back both caches
        rollback(dc, len(seq) - 1)
    return seq[len(ids):len(ids) + n_new]

blocks.md: Two details in the loop. The `for ... else` branch runs only when no guess was rejected, and takes the bonus token from the last distribution. And after a fully accepted round the draft's cache is one token short (it never ran its own last guess), so the next round's first `feed` runs two tokens for it; the invariant makes that automatic.

blocks.prompt: Delete the target's rollback (line 22) and let the next verify pass write after the stale entries, as if the cache were clean. At temperature 0, does the output still equal target.generate?

One drifted after 12 good tokens into 'Johannes Gutenberg invented a book a printing press was used in 140000.0.0.0'. The stale keys and values sit in the attention context as if they were text, and every later position index is shifted, so the target scores guesses after a context that never happened. Nothing crashes; quality just quietly collapses.

blocks.md:
Now check exactness two ways.

1. **Greedy equality**: at temperature 0, with gamma = 4 and 48 new tokens on each of four prompts (prose, a Python docstring, biology, physics), the loop's output was token for token identical to `target.generate(do_sample=False)`.
2. **Distribution test**: at temperature 1, we ran the loop 4,000 times on 'Photosynthesis is the process by which plants' and counted the first output token. The yardstick is total variation (TV) distance, half the summed absolute differences. The loop's frequencies were 0.042 from $p$; 4,000 draws made directly from $p$ were 0.041 from it, which is the noise floor of 4,000 samples. The draft's own $q$ is 0.273 from $p$, so $\beta = 0.727$ at this position.

blocks.md:
Now speed. Same four prompts, 64 new tokens each, temperature 0, gamma from 1 to 8. The pooled acceptance rate (accepted guesses over guesses tested) was 0.84 to 0.86 for every gamma, and the per-position rates stayed between 0.76 and 0.96. Lesson 4's capped-geometric formula predicts tokens per round well: from $\alpha = 0.845$ at gamma = 4 it gives 3.67, and the run averaged 3.73.

Then the two costs, as medians of 40 forward passes at a 33-token context. CPU timings move with machine load, so these are ranges from several runs on this laptop: a target step took 15 to 35 ms and a draft step about half as long, so $c$ was 0.45 to 0.53 (0.47 in the run plotted below), far from the hundredfold size gap Leviathan et al. recommend, because the 135M draft has 30 layers to the target's 32 and on a CPU each layer's fixed overhead dominates. And a target pass over 5 positions took **2.3 to 2.7** plain steps in quiet runs (more under load), never close to 1.

blocks.md: Why is verifying so expensive here? Timing one of the target's MLP matrices (960 by 2,560) shows it: about 18 microseconds for 1 row, but roughly ten to twenty times that (170 to 340 microseconds across runs) for 2 to 16 rows. The CPU library has a fast path for a single vector, so the assumption from lesson 1, that a few rows cost the same as one, fails on this hardware. On a GPU at small batch it holds much better, which is where the papers' 2x to 3x come from. The remaining 10% gap is Python overhead and the draft's occasional two-token step. A second run under background load was slower overall but gave the same shape, with every gamma below 1.

In practice you rarely write this loop. In transformers, speculative decoding is one argument to `generate`, `assistant_model=draft`, and prompt lookup is `prompt_lookup_num_tokens=n`; the docs say speculative decoding supports greedy search and sampling but not batched inputs, and show prompt lookup with both greedy search and sampling. Timed on the same CPU at temperature 0 with 64 new tokens, in three runs:

- Open-ended prompt ('The history of the printing press begins in'): 0.57x to 0.61x with the draft model and 0.48x to 0.73x with prompt lookup. Slower, as the measured costs predict.
- Copy prompt (a paragraph, then 'The same paragraph again, word for word:'): 1.32x to 1.75x with the draft model and **2.31x to 3.40x** with prompt lookup, whose $c$ is nearly 0 and whose guesses are almost always right when the output repeats the input.

Every output was identical to plain greedy generation.

blocks.md: An implementation is four steps: draft with the draft's cache, one target pass, accept or fix up, then roll **both** caches back to the accepted length. Test exactness with greedy equality and a distribution check, then plug measured alpha, c and verify cost into the formula. The verify cost is the term most often assumed and least often checked.

blocks.question: After a rejection, an implementation forgets to roll back the target's KV cache and appends the next round's tokens after the stale entries. What happens?
options: It crashes with a shape mismatch on the next verify pass
Outputs stay correct, but each round wastes a few cache slots
Only sampling is affected; greedy output still matches the target
Outputs silently diverge: the target attends to rejected guesses as if they were text, at shifted positions, so its distributions are wrong

The TV distance between the output and p

lessons.title: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees

blocks.md: A separate draft model is awkward in practice: you need one with the same tokenizer, it has its own KV cache and serving setup, and for a small target there may be no smaller sibling. **Medusa** (Cai et al., 2024) removes the draft model. It adds $K$ extra **decoding heads** (here $K$ counts heads, not Chen's lookahead) on the target's last hidden state $h_t$, the vector the final transformer layer outputs at position $t$. Normally the **LM head** (a linear layer from the hidden size to one score per vocabulary token, then a softmax) turns $h_t$ into the next-token distribution. With Medusa the original LM head still predicts token $t+1$, and head $k$ predicts token $t+k+1$, all from the same forward pass.

Each head is small. It multiplies $h_t$ by its own matrix $W_1$, applies SiLU (the activation $x \cdot \text{sigmoid}(x)$, a smooth version of ReLU), adds $h_t$ back (a residual connection), then multiplies by a second matrix $W_2$ to get one score per vocabulary token, and a softmax turns the scores into the head's distribution, which plays the role of the draft's $q$.

blocks.caption: Each Medusa head is one feed-forward layer with a residual connection. W2 starts as a copy of the LM head and W1 at zero, so heads start out predicting what the base model predicts.

blocks.md: Two training recipes follow. The **backbone** is the target's own stack of transformer layers, everything below the heads; **frozen** means its weights are not updated during training. The paper's test models are Vicuna chat models, which LMSYS fine-tuned from Meta's LLaMA on ShareGPT, a public collection of ChatGPT conversations that users shared.

blocks.title: Medusa: extra heads on the frozen backbone

scenes.caption: A normal decode step: the backbone produces h_t and the LM head predicts the next token.
Medusa heads read the same h_t and guess further ahead. No extra backbone pass: drafting costs only a few small matrix multiplies.
Medusa-1 trains only the heads on a frozen backbone (5 hours for Vicuna-7B on one A100, 60k ShareGPT samples). Medusa-2 also fine-tunes the backbone with a combined loss for better heads.

blocks.md: Head $k$ is guessing a token several positions out without seeing the tokens in between, so its top-1 guess is often wrong. Medusa therefore takes the **top-$s_k$** guesses of each head and forms their Cartesian product, a **token tree**: with $s_1 = 2$ and $s_2 = 3$ there are 2 first-level nodes and $2 \times 3 = 6$ second-level nodes. Level $k$ has $s_1 \times \dots \times s_k$ nodes, because every node on level $k-1$ branches into $s_k$ children, so in general the tree has $\sum_{k=1}^{K} \prod_{i=1}^{k} s_i$ nodes.

To verify all branches in one target pass, flatten the tree into one sequence and replace the causal mask with a **tree attention mask**: each node may attend to the cached prefix and to its own ancestors only, and its position index is its depth. This idea appears in SpecInfer (Miao et al.) and Medusa, and EAGLE uses it too.

blocks.title: Tree attention mask for 2 x 3 candidates (1 = may attend)

scenes.caption: Rows are queries, columns keys, for the 8 tree nodes after the prefix (the prefix itself is visible to all). Level 1 holds head 1's top 2 'It' and 'I'; level 2 holds head 2's top 3 under each.
'is', 'was', 'has' attend to 'It' and themselves, not to 'I' or each other. Each row is exactly the causal mask of one candidate path, so 8 positions verify 6 full paths.
'think' sees only 'I' and itself. Position ids follow depth (0 for It and I, 1 for the rest), so positional encodings match what each path would get as a plain sequence.
Without the tree, these 6 paths would need 6 sequences of length 2, i.e. 12 positions and a batch of 6. The shared first-level tokens are computed once.

blocks.md: After the pass, the engine picks the **longest accepted path**. With greedy decoding that is the deepest branch whose tokens all match the target's argmax. With sampling you need a tree version of the rejection rule. SpecInfer's multi-step speculative sampling tries a node's children one at a time: accept child $x$ with probability $\min(1, p(x)/q(x))$; on rejection, replace $p$ by $\text{norm}(\max(0, p - q))$ and try the next child; if all children fail, sample from what is left of $p$. SpecInfer proves this still yields exactly the target distribution.

A worked example, reusing the toy vocabulary from lesson 3: target $p = (0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1)$ over {the, a, cat, dog} and draft $q = (0.3, 0.4, 0.1, 0.2)$. The node has **two** candidate children, each an independent sample from $q$, and SpecInfer tries them one at a time. Say child 1 is 'a' and child 2 is 'dog'.

1. Test 'a' against $p$: accept with $\min(1, 0.2/0.4) = 0.5$. Suppose it is rejected.
2. Replace $p$ by the residual $p_1 = \text{norm}(\max(0, p - q)) = (2/3, 0, 1/3, 0)$.
3. Test 'dog' against $p_1$, not $p$: $p_1(\text{dog}) = 0$, so it is always rejected. Update again: $p_2 = \text{norm}(\max(0, p_1 - q)) = (0.611, 0, 0.389, 0)$.
4. No children left: sample the output from $p_2$.

blocks.title: Two children, one node: multi-step speculative sampling

scenes.caption: Target p = (0.5, 0.2, 0.2, 0.1) and draft q = (0.3, 0.4, 0.1, 0.2), the pair from lesson 3. Both children are independent samples from q.
Child 1 'a' is rejected (it had a 0.5 chance). The target is replaced by the residual p1 = (2/3, 0, 1/3, 0): exactly the mass the draft under-covers.
Child 2 is tested against p1 with min(1, p1/q) = (1, 0, 1, 0). 'the' or 'cat' would be kept for sure; 'dog' is rejected, and p1 shrinks again to p2 = (0.611, 0, 0.389, 0).
Over all draws the output is exactly p. A 200,000-run simulation gives 0.5004, 0.1998, 0.1996, 0.1001. With two children some child is accepted 82% of the time, against 70% with one.

blocks.md: Why the second child is tested against $p_1$: once child 1 is rejected, the output must follow the residual, so the second test is an ordinary speculative-sampling step whose target is $p_1$. Each step is exact for its own target, so the chain is exact for $p$. The gain is acceptance: the chance that some child survives rises from 0.7 to $0.7 + 0.3 \times 0.4 = 0.82$, where 0.4 is $\sum_x \min(p_1(x), q(x))$. SpecInfer reports that this beats naive sampling (sample from $p$, then look for the token in the tree), verifying 1.2x to 1.3x more tokens per step.

Medusa also offers a shortcut that is not exact. **Entropy** $H(p) = -\sum_x p(x) \log p(x)$ measures how spread out a distribution is: 0 when one token holds all the probability, and the log of the vocabulary size when every token is equally likely. Medusa's **typical acceptance** compares the target's probability of a candidate with a threshold built from two tuned constants, a hard threshold $\epsilon$ and an entropy-dependent threshold $\delta$ times $e^{-H}$. When the target is unsure, $H$ is large, the bar drops, and more candidates pass.

Not every tree method is lossless. Medusa's optional **typical acceptance** keeps a candidate if the target's probability exceeds $\min(\epsilon, \delta e^{-H(p)})$, a threshold that depends on the entropy $H$. It raises speed at higher temperatures but no longer samples from the target's distribution. Medusa-2 also changes the backbone weights, so outputs differ from the original model.

Reported results: Medusa-1 gives over 2.2x speedup on Vicuna models without changing outputs, and Medusa-2 gives 2.3x to 2.8x (Cai et al., on MT-Bench, a benchmark of 80 multi-turn conversation questions from LMSYS). The paper recommends training 5 heads and tuning a sparse tree, one that keeps only the most promising branches instead of the full Cartesian product; their tuned tree for Medusa-2 Vicuna-7B has 64 nodes and depth 4.

blocks.question: With s1 = 3, s2 = 2, s3 = 2, how many tree nodes must the target verify in one pass?
blocks.explain: Level sizes are 3, 3 x 2 = 6 and 3 x 2 x 2 = 12, for 3 + 6 + 12 = 21 nodes. Twelve full candidate paths share their prefixes, which is why tree attention is cheaper than 12 separate sequences of length 3.

blocks.question: In multi-step speculative sampling, child 1 was rejected. A teammate tests child 2 with min(1, p(x)/q(x)) using the original p. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; every child is compared with the same target p
Child 2 should be compared with q only
After the rejection the output must follow the residual p1, so child 2 must be tested against p1; using p over-weights tokens the draft over-proposes
Child 2 should always be accepted after a rejection
blocks.explain: The rejection already spent the accepted mass min(p, q). What remains to be produced is the residual p1 = norm(max(0, p - q)). Testing against p would add min(p, q) a second time, the same double counting as resampling from p in lesson 3.

blocks.question: A tree-attention kernel accidentally uses the ordinary causal mask on the flattened tree. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; causal masking is a superset of tree masking
Only the position ids are off by one
The pass becomes slower but results are identical
Each node also attends to earlier sibling branches, so the target scores tokens in contexts that never occur and verification becomes wrong
blocks.explain: Under a causal mask 'think' would attend to 'It', 'is', 'was' and so on, a context that is not its real prefix. Its distribution is then wrong and so are the accept and reject decisions. The mask must restrict attention to ancestors.

lessons.title: EAGLE drafts and prompt lookup decoding

blocks.md: **EAGLE** (Li et al., 2024) keeps a small autoregressive drafter but feeds it the target's own **features**, the second-to-top-layer hidden states before the LM head. The drafter is one FC (fully connected, that is, linear) layer plus one transformer decoder layer, and it reuses the target's embedding and LM head. It is trained to predict the target's next feature vector, scored by a regression loss (smooth L1, a distance between predicted and true features), plus a cross-entropy loss on the token that the predicted feature gives through the LM head.

Its input is the feature sequence together with the token sequence shifted one step ahead, so it knows which token was actually sampled. Why that matters: a feature fixes a distribution, not a token. After 'I' the target might sample 'am' or 'always', and the next feature differs between the two, so features alone leave the drafter guessing which branch happened. The paper reports this fixes the uncertainty of predicting features alone.

The EAGLE drafter is cheap to build: 0.24B trainable parameters for a 7B target and 0.99B for 70B, trained on a fixed ShareGPT dataset in 1 to 2 days on four A100 (40 GB) GPUs, even for the 70B models. It drafts a tree and verifies with tree attention and the lossless sampling rule, reporting 2.7x to 3.5x latency speedup for LLaMA2-Chat 70B.

**EAGLE-2** observed that the drafter is well calibrated (its confidence matches how often it is right): draft tokens with confidence below 0.05 were accepted about 4% of the time, those above 0.95 about 98%. So it grows a **dynamic tree**: the value of a node is the product of confidences along its path (an estimate that the whole path is accepted), it expands the top-k nodes per level, then reranks all nodes and keeps the top m. Reported speedups are 3.05x to 4.26x, 20% to 40% faster than EAGLE-1.

blocks.title: EAGLE-2 dynamic draft tree (example from the paper)

scenes.caption: Layer 1: the drafter proposes 'is' (confidence 0.6) and 'has' (0.2). A node's value is the product of confidences on its path.
Layer 2 values: a 0.48, the 0.06, to 0.14, a 0.02. EAGLE-2 expands only the top 2 by value, 'a' and 'to', instead of every node.
Layer 3 values: good 0.336, nice 0.048, be 0.084, do 0.028. Deeper nodes have lower values because every factor is at most 1.

Rerank: keep the 8 highest values, counting the root 'It' (value 1) as the paper's figure does. The shallow 'the' (0.06) beats the deeper 'nice' (0.048) and 'do'. A child never outranks its parent, so the kept set is a connected tree.

blocks.md: **EAGLE-3** found that adding training data helped EAGLE little, and blamed the feature-prediction loss (the regression term above). It drops that loss and predicts tokens directly, and instead of the top layer it concatenates **low, middle and high** layer features of the target (3 times the hidden size) and projects them back with an FC layer. Because drafted positions have no target features, training feeds the drafter its own outputs, a technique the authors call **training-time test**. The paper reports up to 6.5x speedup, about 1.4x over EAGLE-2, and 1.38x throughput at batch size 64 in SGLang, an open-source LLM serving engine (vLLM, used in lesson 9, is another).

What training-time test fixes is a form of **exposure bias**: a model trained only on ground-truth inputs is tested on its own outputs. In the EAGLE-3 paper's example the text so far is 'How can' and the target has just sampled 'I'. Step 1 reads the target's features $g$ for 'How' and 'can' plus the embedding of 'I', and outputs a vector $a_{\text{I}}$ that gives the draft token 'do'. At step 2 the target has not processed 'I' yet, so there is no target feature for it; the drafter must use its own $a_{\text{I}}$ in its place. A drafter trained only on target features meets inputs at step 2 that it never saw in training, and the paper shows EAGLE's acceptance rate falling as more of its input comes from its own estimates.

blocks.title: What the drafter reads at each step (example from EAGLE-3)

scenes.caption: Plain training: every input is a target feature g, because the whole training sequence has already been through the target.
Inference, step 2: the target sampled 'I' but has not run on it yet, so the slot for 'I' holds the drafter's own output a_I. Training never showed the drafter such an input.
Step 3 is worse: two of the inputs are the drafter's own estimates. Errors compound, so later draft positions are accepted less often.
Training-time test runs the drafter's own steps during training too: its outputs a are fed back in, with matching attention masks, so the inputs at steps 2 and 3 look like inference.

blocks.md: The cheapest drafter is no model at all. **Prompt lookup decoding** (an n-gram drafter) takes the last few generated tokens, searches for the same n-gram (a run of n consecutive tokens) earlier in the prompt or output, and proposes the tokens that followed it. Its cost ratio $c$ is essentially 0, so speedup is just tokens per pass. It shines when outputs copy the input: summarization, document QA, code edits.

blocks.title: Prompt lookup with a 3-token n-gram

scenes.caption: The generated text ends with 'total cost of'. Take this 3-token suffix as the search key.
An earlier occurrence sits at positions 0 to 2. No model ran; this is a string search over token ids.
Copy the 4 tokens that followed the match as draft guesses. The target verifies them exactly as it would a model's guesses, so a wrong copy costs one round but never changes the output.

blocks.md: The prompt-lookup reference implementation reports about 2.4x average speedup on summarization and context QA with Mistral-7B-Instruct at greedy decoding on one A100, and much less on open-ended chat with short prompts. It ships in Hugging Face transformers as `prompt_lookup_num_tokens` and in vLLM as the `ngram` method.

All variants share one loop: draft cheaply (small model, extra heads, feature-level head, or string lookup), verify a chain or tree in one target pass, keep the accepted prefix plus one target token. They differ only in how they guess, and that sets alpha and c.

blocks.question: Which drafter fits best for an assistant that rewrites long user-provided code files with small edits, given no budget to train anything?
options: Prompt lookup (n-gram) drafting
A freshly trained EAGLE-3 head
Medusa-2 with a fine-tuned backbone
Typical acceptance with a high threshold
blocks.explain: The output copies long spans of the input, which is exactly what n-gram lookup predicts, and it needs no training and costs almost nothing per guess (c near 0). Medusa-2 and typical acceptance also change outputs.

blocks.question: Medusa's typical acceptance, Medusa-2, EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup: which of these can change the output distribution compared to the original target model?
options: Only EAGLE-2
Typical acceptance and Medusa-2
Prompt lookup, because copied tokens skip the target
All four
blocks.explain: Typical acceptance replaces rejection sampling with a threshold, and Medusa-2 fine-tunes the backbone itself. EAGLE-2 and prompt lookup only change how drafts are proposed; verification with the standard rule keeps the target's distribution.

blocks.question: An EAGLE-1-style drafter has a high acceptance rate at draft position 1 but much lower at positions 3 and 4. Which explanation fits best?
options: The target's LM head is less accurate deep into a draft
Exposure bias: from step 2 on, the drafter's inputs include its own predicted features, which it never saw in training, and errors compound
Tree attention masks hide earlier draft tokens
Position 1 is always accepted because it is the bonus token
blocks.explain: Each later step feeds the drafter its own estimates instead of target features. EAGLE-3's training-time test simulates those steps during training, and the paper reports its acceptance rate stays almost flat as more inputs come from the drafter.

lessons.title: Self-speculation: MTP heads, layer skipping and lookahead

blocks.md: Every drafter so far except prompt lookup is something extra to train, store and serve. **Self-speculation** drafts with the target itself, using a cheaper partial pass of the same network. A tiny example: a 32-layer model guesses the next 4 tokens using only its first 8 layers, then runs all 32 layers once to check them. Three families do this, each with its own trade-off between acceptance rate $\alpha$ and cost ratio $c$: extra prediction modules trained into the model, skipping layers, and guessing many positions at once with Jacobi iteration.

blocks.title: Where the draft comes from

scenes.caption: Every method feeds the same verify step. They differ only in where guesses come from, which sets alpha and c.
Lessons 1 to 7: a separate model, or small heads added beside a frozen or fine-tuned target. All add parameters that must be trained.
MTP modules are trained together with the model in pretraining, so they ship with the checkpoint and cost little to run as a drafter.
Layer skipping drafts with part of the target's own stack: no new weights at all. Draft & Verify needs no training; LayerSkip retrains the model to make early exits accurate.
Lookahead decoding drafts from n-grams collected while the target itself runs Jacobi iterations in the same pass: no draft model, no training.

blocks.md: **Multi-token prediction (MTP)** is covered in depth by the optional *Multi-token prediction* course (DeepSeek-V3's modules in its lesson 4, decoding with them in its lesson 7); here is all this course needs. DeepSeek-V3 trains **sequential** MTP modules: module $k$ combines the representation from depth $k-1$ (the main model's hidden state when $k = 1$) with the embedding of the token $k$ positions ahead, keeping the causal chain. Medusa's heads, by contrast, all read the same $h_t$ in parallel (lesson 6). At inference the module can be dropped or reused as a drafter. The report gives an 85% to 90% acceptance rate for the second token and about 1.8x the tokens per second. With $\gamma = 1$, lesson 4's formula gives $1 + 0.85 = 1.85$ tokens per target pass at the low end, so the measured 1.8x is close to the ceiling.

**Layer skipping** needs no new weights. **Draft & Verify** (Zhang et al., 2023) drafts by running the target with some intermediate attention and MLP layers skipped, chosen by Bayesian optimization (a search method for expensive black-box functions) to minimize time per verified token on a development set. It also stops drafting early when the draft's confidence falls below a threshold that adapts to the observed acceptance. The method needs no training and no extra memory and reports up to 1.99x on LLaMA-2 models.

**LayerSkip** (Elhoushi et al., 2024) drafts with the first $E$ of $L$ layers, then runs the remaining $L - E$ layers to verify. Draft and verify share the first $E$ layers, so there is **one KV cache**, and an exit query cache lets verification continue from layer $E$ instead of recomputing the early layers. It reports 1.34x to 2.16x depending on the task.

The catch: an LM head is trained to read the **last** layer. Exiting early from an unmodified model gives poor guesses. We measured this on SmolLM2-360M (32 layers): over 191 tokens of its own greedy text, we applied the final norm and LM head to the hidden state after $E$ layers and counted how often the argmax matched the full model's, which is the greedy acceptance rate of a one-token early-exit draft.

blocks.title: Early exit on an untrained model: agreement with the last layer

scenes.caption: Exiting after 8 or 16 layers agrees with the full model on only 8% and 13% of tokens: useless as a draft.
Agreement climbs only near the end: 28% after 24 layers, 47% after 28, 64% after 31 of 32. A draft cheap enough to help is too inaccurate.

blocks.md: That is why LayerSkip changes training. **Layer dropout** skips each layer at random during training, with low rates for early layers and higher rates for later ones, so the network learns not to depend on every layer. An **early exit loss** applies the shared LM head to every layer's output, so early layers learn to produce readable predictions. The result is one set of weights with accurate sub-models at many depths. Like Medusa-2, this changes the backbone weights: the model you serve is the retrained one, and speculation is exact with respect to it.

blocks.title: Layer-skip drafting: speedup vs draft depth E / L

x.label: draft depth E / L (cost ratio c)

curves.label: shared layers: cost gamma c + 1 - c

scenes.caption: Simplified: draft cost proportional to depth, alpha held fixed. With alpha = 0.8 and gamma = 4, drafting with a quarter of the layers gives 1.68x; reusing those layers in verification lifts it to 1.92x.
In reality alpha rises with E. With the untrained exits measured above (alpha about 0.47 at E / L = 0.875), even the shared version stays below 1.
A well-trained early exit (alpha 0.9) at a quarter depth: 2.34x with shared layers. Training for early exits is what makes self-drafting pay.

blocks.md: **Jacobi decoding** removes the drafter entirely. Greedy decoding solves $m$ equations one at a time: $y_1$ is the argmax after the prompt, $y_2$ the argmax after the prompt and $y_1$, and so on. Jacobi iteration instead guesses all $m$ tokens, runs one forward pass over all of them, replaces every guess with the argmax at its position, and repeats until nothing changes. After each pass the first wrong position has a fully correct prefix, so it becomes right; every pass fixes at least one more token, so Jacobi never takes more than $m$ passes and ends at exactly the greedy output. We ran it on SmolLM2-360M with 8 positions, all initialised to '.', after 'The three laws of motion described by Isaac Newton are':

blocks.title: Jacobi iterations on SmolLM2-360M (8 positions)

scenes.caption: Start: 8 placeholder tokens. The bottom row is what plain greedy decoding produces (NL is a newline).
Pass 1: every position gets the argmax given the guesses before it. Only position 0 is right; the rest condition on placeholders.
Pass 2: positions 0 and 1 are right. Later positions hold fragments such as 'Newton' that are plausible but in the wrong place.
Pass 5: five right. Each pass fixed exactly one more token, so 8 passes for 8 tokens: no fewer steps than greedy decoding.
Pass 8: converged to the greedy answer. The lookahead paper reports the same: plain Jacobi decoding rarely fixes more than one token per step.

blocks.md: **Lookahead decoding** (Fu et al., 2024) keeps Jacobi's parallel guessing but stops expecting tokens to land in the right place. Its **lookahead branch** runs Jacobi-style updates over a window of $W$ future positions, using the last $N - 1$ steps of the trajectory, and collects the $n$-grams that appear along it into an **n-gram pool**. Its **verification branch** takes up to $G$ pool entries that start with the current last token and verifies them like draft continuations. Both branches run in the same forward pass, so the spare compute of a memory-bound step pays for them. No draft model, no training, exact output (sampling is supported too). The paper reports 1.8x on MT-Bench and up to 4x on code completion with Lookahead Parallelism on 8 GPUs.

Lesson 3 showed that $\alpha = 1 - $ the average TV distance between $p$ and $q$, and lesson 4 that $\alpha$ is the lever that matters most. **DistillSpec** (Zhou et al., 2023) raises it by distilling the draft toward the target before speculating. Its two design choices: train on **on-policy** data, sequences generated by the draft itself and scored by the target, and tune the divergence to the task and decoding mode, since minimizing TV directly was not always best. It reports 10% to 45% speedups over standard speculative decoding across a range of benchmarks. How on-policy distillation works is in lesson 7 of the *Knowledge distillation* course.

Self-speculation trades a separate draft for a cheaper pass of the target: MTP modules built into training, a subset of layers, or n-grams harvested from Jacobi iterations. Cheap drafts only help if they agree with the full model, so the methods that pay off either train for it (MTP, LayerSkip) or search for it (Draft & Verify, lookahead).

blocks.question: Which two methods need no extra parameters and no training at all?
options: Medusa-1 and EAGLE-3
MTP drafting and LayerSkip
Lookahead decoding and prompt lookup
DistillSpec and Medusa-2
blocks.explain: Lookahead builds its n-gram pool from the target's own Jacobi iterations, and prompt lookup copies n-grams from the context. Medusa and EAGLE train heads, MTP modules are trained with the model, LayerSkip retrains it, and DistillSpec trains the draft.

blocks.question: Which method changes the weights of the backbone you end up serving?
options: Draft & Verify, because it skips layers
LayerSkip, whose layer dropout and early exit loss retrain the model, much like Medusa-2's fine-tuning
Lookahead decoding, because it updates the n-gram pool
Prompt lookup decoding
blocks.explain: Draft & Verify only skips layers at inference time, and lookahead and prompt lookup change no weights. LayerSkip trains (or continues pretraining) the model itself, so outputs are exact with respect to the retrained model, not the original one.

blocks.question: A team drafts with the first 16 of 32 layers of an off-the-shelf model, with no retraining, and sees almost no accepted tokens. What is the most likely reason?
options: The LM head was trained to read only the last layer's output, so early hidden states give poor predictions
Early layers cannot use the KV cache
The verify pass must also stop at layer 16
Greedy decoding cannot be used with layer skipping
blocks.explain: On SmolLM2-360M an exit after 16 of 32 layers matched the full model on 13% of tokens. LayerSkip adds an early exit loss so the shared LM head learns to read earlier layers.

lessons.title: Speculation in a serving system: batch size, long context and tuning

blocks.md: Everything so far assumed one request. A server decodes a **batch** of requests in every step and refills it as requests finish (continuous batching, lesson 6 of GPU and inference basics; the *LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management* course covers the scheduler). Speculation changes what a step contains: each sequence now brings $\gamma + 1$ positions to verify instead of 1, so a batch of $B$ requests sends $B(\gamma + 1)$ token rows through every weight matrix. Whether that is still nearly free depends on where the step sits on the roofline.

When does it pay off? The vLLM docs say speculative decoding reduces inter-token latency (the time between consecutive output tokens) for **medium-to-low QPS** (queries per second), **memory-bound** workloads. At high load the batch already keeps the GPU busy with useful arithmetic, so the extra verification work (lesson 4: 1.63x the operations at alpha 0.8, gamma 5) competes with other requests instead of filling idle cycles.

blocks.caption: The step model from GPU and inference basics (lesson 6) with B(gamma + 1) token rows instead of B. The memory term does not change: weights and each sequence's KV cache are read once however many positions are verified. Attention FLOPs and overheads ignored.

blocks.md:
Numbers from that course: LLaMA-7B in FP16 on an A100 reads 13.4 GB of weights per step (6.57 ms), and each token row costs 0.043 ms of math at peak. Take $\gamma = 4$, so 5 rows per sequence, and ignore context for now:

- $B = 1$: 5 rows, 0.21 ms of math against 6.57 ms of reads. Verify costs one step.
- $B = 16$: 80 rows, 3.44 ms of math. Still one step.
- $B = 64$: 320 rows, 13.7 ms of math. The verify pass is now compute bound and costs 2.09 plain steps, while plain decoding at $B = 64$ (2.75 ms of math) is still memory bound.

The crossover is where $B(\gamma + 1)$ reaches the ridge of about 153 rows: $B \approx 31$ for $\gamma = 4$. Plain decoding would stay memory bound until $B \approx 153$, so speculation runs out of free compute five times sooner.

blocks.prompt: Same setup, with alpha = 0.8 (3.36 tokens per round, lesson 4) and a draft costing c = 0.05 per step. Using speedup = tokens per round / (gamma c + T_verify / T_step), estimate the speedup at B = 64 and at B = 128.
blocks.reveal: At $B = 64$ the verify pass costs 2.09 steps: $3.36 / (0.2 + 2.09) = 1.47$x, about half of the 2.80x at small batch. At $B = 128$ the pass does 640 rows, 27.5 ms against a 6.57 ms plain step, a ratio of 4.18: $3.36 / (0.2 + 4.18) = 0.77$x. Speculation now makes every user **slower**, although the acceptance rate never changed.

blocks.title: Modelled speedup vs batch size: LLaMA-7B, A100, gamma = 4

scenes.caption: No context: flat at 2.80x until B is about 31, where verifying 5 rows per sequence hits the compute roof. It crosses 1 near B = 97. Simplified: c fixed at 0.05, overheads ignored.
1,024 tokens of context: each sequence's 512 MiB cache read (0.26 ms) outweighs its 0.21 ms of verify math, so the step stays memory bound at every batch size and the speedup holds.
Weaker draft, alpha = 0.6, no context: 2.31 tokens per round. The small-batch speedup is lower and the curve falls below 1 sooner, near B = 65.
The model ignores memory capacity: at 4,096 tokens only about 31 sequences fit on an 80 GB A100 (GPU basics, lesson 5), so the right part of this curve is not reachable there.

blocks.md: The second scene is the counter-case that **MagicDec** (Sadhukhan et al., 2024) measured. With long sequences the KV cache, not the weights, dominates each step, and every sequence brings its own cache, so the bytes grow with batch size as fast as the FLOPs do. Verify and plain decoding read the same cache, so their ratio stays near 1 even at large batch. In the model above, verification stays memory bound at any batch once $n_{\text{ctx}}\, s_{\text{kv}} / \text{bandwidth} \ge (\gamma + 1)\, 2N / \text{peak}$: about 835 tokens of context for LLaMA-7B with $\gamma = 4$. Grouped-query attention shrinks $s_{\text{kv}}$, which raises this threshold; the paper notes that GQA models need longer sequences for the effect.

blocks.title: MagicDec on 8 A100s: LLaMA-2-7B-32K, TinyLlama draft, gamma 2

scenes.caption: Verify time over plain decode time (T_V / T_AR) from the paper's raw table. At 1,024 tokens it rises with batch to 1.35; at 8,000 tokens it stays near 1.1 and even falls.

Measured speedup. Short sequences: 0.94x to 1.01x, no gain. Long sequences: 1.27x at batch 32 rising to 1.60x at batch 128, because the draft's small fixed KV cache gets relatively cheaper as the target's grows.

blocks.md: MagicDec's drafts use a small, fixed KV budget instead of the whole context, for example 512 tokens chosen StreamingLLM-style (the first few tokens, which attention leans on as 'sinks', plus a window of the most recent ones), so drafting does not grow with context length. In the bars above the draft is TinyLlama-1.1B, a small open model that shares LLaMA 2's tokenizer. With the target itself as the draft (self-speculation with a sparse KV cache) the paper reports up to 2.51x for LLaMA-3.1-8B on 8 H100s at batch sizes 32 to 256. Not run here: these are multi-GPU measurements from the paper's appendix.

Batching also makes the bookkeeping ragged. In one step, request A may accept 0 drafts, B 2 and C all 4, so their sequences grow by 1, 3 and 5 tokens. Each request keeps its own length, so the engine tracks acceptance per request. Before the step every draft needs a cache slot: in vLLM's KV manager a step's new tokens include the unverified drafts, and extra lookahead slots are reserved for drafters with their own cache, such as EAGLE. After it, rollback is cheap: in vLLM's scheduler it is one subtraction, `num_computed_tokens -= num_rejected`, so the rejected entries sit past the sequence's end and the next step overwrites them. Prefix caching (reusing stored keys and values when a new request shares a prefix with an earlier one) only stores verified tokens. How blocks and block tables work is the subject of the *PagedAttention and prefix caching* course.

blocks.title: One batched verify step: three requests accept 1, 3 and 5 tokens

scenes.caption: Each request scores 5 positions: its 4 drafts plus the bonus position after them. Its last accepted token and the 4 drafts go in as 5 rows (15 in all, one pass) and write 5 cache entries.
Verification: A rejects its first draft (1 token: the fix-up), B keeps 2 drafts plus a fix-up (3 tokens), C keeps all 4 plus the bonus (5 tokens).

Rollback is bookkeeping: each request's length advances by 1, 3 or 5, and the slots past it are free for the next step to overwrite. The fix-up and bonus tokens get their cache entries in the next pass.

blocks.md: Because the best $\gamma$ falls as the batch grows, engines adjust it online. vLLM's dynamic speculative decoding takes a schedule of concurrency ranges, each with its own number of draft tokens. The docs give the reason in one line: verification turns batch size $B$ into an effective $B \times K$, and past a critical batch size speculation slows decoding (TPOT). Their EAGLE example drafts 3 tokens up to 64 concurrent requests, 1 token from 65 to 128, and none beyond 128.

In vLLM you enable speculation with a `speculative_config`. Among the methods the docs list are model-based ones (EAGLE; MTP heads, the multi-token prediction layers that some models such as DeepSeek-V3 are trained with to predict several future tokens; a separate draft model) and model-free ones (n-gram; suffix decoding, which matches the current text against suffix trees built from the prompt and earlier responses). The examples below follow the vLLM docs; check them for current options and supported model pairs.

blocks.code:
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

# EAGLE-3 draft head (example from the vLLM docs)
llm = LLM(
    model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct",
    tensor_parallel_size=2,
    speculative_config={
        "model": "RedHatAI/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-speculator.eagle3",
        "draft_tensor_parallel_size": 2,
        "num_speculative_tokens": 2,
        "method": "eagle3",
    },
)

# Draft-free alternative: prompt lookup (n-gram)
llm_ngram = LLM(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    speculative_config={
        "method": "ngram",
        "num_speculative_tokens": 5,
        "prompt_lookup_max": 4,
    },
)
out = llm.generate(["Summarize: ..."], SamplingParams(temperature=0.8))
blocks.caption: num_speculative_tokens is gamma. The draft head is trained for a specific target model family; the vLLM EAGLE page lists pre-trained heads for common targets. tensor_parallel_size=2 splits each weight matrix across 2 GPUs, which is where lesson 1's all-reduces come from.

blocks.code:
# Dynamic speculation length (vLLM dynamic speculative decoding docs)
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --speculative-config '{
    "method": "eagle",
    "model": "yuhuili/EAGLE-LLaMA3.1-Instruct-8B",
    "num_speculative_tokens": 3,
    "num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size": [[1, 64, 3], [65, 128, 1], [129, 512, 0]]
  }'

# What to watch on /metrics (counters, one value per draft position)
#   vllm:spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens_per_pos
#   vllm:spec_decode_num_verified_tokens_per_pos
# per-position acceptance = accepted / verified at that position
blocks.caption: Not run here (needs an NVIDIA GPU). Config from the vLLM dynamic speculative decoding page, metric names from the vLLM metrics page; both change between releases, so check the current docs.

blocks.md:
What to monitor:

- **Mean acceptance length**: tokens emitted per verify step including the bonus, $1 + \text{accepted} / \text{steps}$. vLLM can return it per request (`--per-request-spec-decode-metrics`). It measures the draft, not the speedup.
- **Per-position acceptance rate**: accepted over verified at draft position 1, 2, 3 and so on. A steep fall with position says a shorter $\gamma$ would waste less.
- **ITL (TPOT) at a fixed request rate, with and without speculation.** This is the number users feel. Acceptance can stay constant while ITL gets worse, because load moved the verify pass across the ridge.

vLLM documents its rejection sampler as lossless up to hardware numerics, tested with convergence tests (samples match the target distribution) and greedy-equality tests (greedy output is identical with and without speculation), while noting that batch size changes can shift logprobs (the per-token log probabilities a server can return). Its FLy verification mode deliberately relaxes verification and is explicitly not distribution preserving, like Medusa's typical acceptance.

Speculation spends spare compute to save sequential steps. At small batch or long context the verify pass rides on memory reads that happen anyway; once $B(\gamma + 1)$ token rows reach the ridge, every rejected draft costs real time. Shrink $\gamma$ under load, and judge by ITL at fixed load, not by acceptance alone.

blocks.question: A chat service with short prompts runs EAGLE with gamma = 4. After traffic doubled, the mean acceptance length is unchanged but the ITL gain from speculation disappeared. What is the most likely cause?
options: The draft head drifted and now proposes worse tokens
Larger batches pushed B x (gamma + 1) token rows past the ridge, so each verify pass now costs several plain steps
The KV cache of rejected tokens is no longer freed
Acceptance length always falls when traffic rises, so the metric must be broken
blocks.explain: Acceptance length measures the draft, and it did not change. What changed is the cost of a verify pass: with short contexts the step becomes compute bound once B(gamma + 1) approaches about 153 rows on an A100. Lowering gamma under load (dynamic speculation) or disabling it at high concurrency recovers the loss.

blocks.question: A service runs a 70B chat model at very high request rate with large batches and the GPUs are compute bound. Would enabling EAGLE likely cut cost per token?
options: Yes, speculation always reduces work per token
Probably not: the batch already uses the compute, and rejected draft tokens add verification work that competes with other requests
Yes, because EAGLE heads replace the target's LM head
No, because EAGLE cannot run with batch sizes above 1
blocks.explain: Speculation turns idle compute into fewer sequential steps. When the GPU is already compute bound, wasted verification is real cost. vLLM documents the biggest gains at medium-to-low QPS; EAGLE-3 still reports some throughput gain at batch 64 in SGLang, so measure your workload.

blocks.question: Two deployments of the same 8B model see heavy traffic with large batches. One serves 32K-token document QA, the other 200-token chat turns. Where is speculation more likely to still help, and why?
options: Chat, because short sequences have higher acceptance
Neither; speculation never helps at large batch
Both equally, because acceptance rate is all that matters
Document QA: KV-cache reads dominate each step, so the verify pass stays memory bound and costs about one step even at large batch
blocks.explain: At long context each sequence's cache read is far larger than the extra verify arithmetic, so the step stays memory bound as the batch grows (MagicDec's measurements show speedup rising with batch at 8K tokens and above). Short chat turns hit the compute roof first.
